claim: Skeletal elements are resorbed upon amputation in axolotl limbs.
source: To determine the changes in the skeleton upon amputation, we used the stable calcium-binding dyes calcein and alizarin red. These dyes label mineralized cartilage in juvenile axolotls, allowing in vivo imaging (Riquelme-Guzmán et al., 2021). Using 4–6 cm snout-to-tail (ST) axolotls, we amputated the zeugopod at the distal end of the calcified tissue and imaged at different days post amputation (dpa) (Figure 1A). We observed a consistent reduction in the calcein+ tissue from 7 to 12 dpa.
evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging data showing reduction in calcein+ tissue from 7 to 12 dpa, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: By 12 dpa, over 40% of the calcified radius and 60% of the calcified ulna were resorbed.
source: Resorption initiated after 7 dpa and by 12 dpa, over 40% of the calcified radius and 60% of the calcified ulna were resorbed (length resorbed radius: 342.83±95.75 µm; ulna: 770.67±94.34 µm).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of skeletal element lengths at different time points.

claim: The median resorption rate is 40% for radius and 60% for ulna across multiple experiments.
source: We pooled five independent experiments and noticed an important variability between assays (Figure 1C, each color represents an assay). The median for radius resorption is 40% and for ulna 60%; however, in several cases the calcified tissue was completely resorbed in both elements.
evidence: Supported by pooled data from five independent experiments showing median resorption rates.

claim: Skeletal resorption occurs in digit regeneration with similar dynamics to zeugopod regeneration.
source: Similar to the zeugopod, we quantified the calcein+ tissue length at different dpa and revealed a similar trend in the resorptive dynamics: resorption starting after 7 dpa and receding by 13 dpa (Figure 1E), vanishing over 50% of the calcified tissue length (320.43±113.56 µm).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of calcified tissue length in digit regeneration experiments.

claim: Skeletal shedding, including breaks in the ulna, occasionally occurs during resorption.
source: At 9 dpa, we observed resorption in both radius and ulna. Remarkably, we occasionally observed a break in the ulna (Figure 1F arrowhead) that sometimes led to the extrusion of the skeletal fragment through the epidermis. This skeletal shedding was observed both in digit and limb amputations.
evidence: Supported by alcian blue staining observations at 9 dpa showing breaks in skeletal elements.

claim: Osteoclasts are responsible for skeletal resorption during axolotl limb regeneration.
source: Osteoclasts are specialized multinucleated cells responsible for skeletal resorption (Charles and Aliprantis, 2014). Despite their critical role in skeletal biology, osteoclasts have only been reported on the basis of morphology during salamander regeneration (Fischman and Hay, 1962; Nguyen et al., 2017; Tank et al., 1976). Therefore, we sought to identify osteoclasts during resorption using various molecular markers.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about osteoclast function and subsequent identification using molecular markers.

claim: CTSK+ cells are identified adjacent to or inside the calcified skeleton at 8 dpa.
source: Using sections from zeugopodial amputations, we performed immunofluorescence (IF) using an anti-CTSK antibody (Figure 2A) and TRAP enzymatic staining (Figure 2B). CTSK+ cells were identified in sections at 8 dpa adjacent or inside the calcein+ skeleton.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing CTSK+ cells at 8 dpa.

claim: TRAP+ cells are identified at 9 dpa during skeletal resorption.
source: Using sections from zeugopodial amputations, we performed immunofluorescence (IF) using an anti-CTSK antibody (Figure 2A) and TRAP enzymatic staining (Figure 2B). CTSK+ cells were identified in sections at 8 dpa adjacent or inside the calcein+ skeleton. Similarly, TRAP+ cells were identified at 9 dpa.
evidence: Supported by TRAP enzymatic staining showing TRAP+ cells at 9 dpa.

claim: RNA expression of Trap, Ctsk, and Dcstamp peaks at 9 dpa and rapidly decreases to basal levels by 15 dpa.
source: Next, to correlate osteoclast recruitment with resorption timing, we performed RT-qPCR at different dpa using specific primers for Trap, Ctsk, and Dcstamp (dendritic cell-specific transmembrane protein, involved in osteoclast multinucleation). The RNA relative content for the three markers behaved similarly: a sharp increase was observed, reaching a peak at 9 dpa before rapidly decrease to almost basal levels at 15 dpa (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data showing temporal expression patterns of osteoclast markers.

claim: Ctsk:mRuby3+ cells are absent at 0 dpa and appear as mononuclear cells at 9 dpa in the periphery of the calcified phalanx.
source: Using our Ctsk:mRuby3 line, we followed resorption in vivo in digits with confocal microscopy (Figure 2D, two independent experiments). At 0 dpa, the tissue was devoid of mRuby3+ cells. At 9 dpa, mononuclear-like mRuby3 + cells were observed in the periphery of the calcified phalanx.
evidence: Supported by in vivo confocal imaging data of Ctsk:mRuby3 transgenic line.

claim: Ctsk:mRuby3+ cells become multinucleated at 11 dpa during skeletal resorption.
source: These cells increased in numbers and became multinucleated at 11 dpa (white arrowheads). A piece of the calcified structure (black arrowhead) has been detached at this timepoint.
evidence: Supported by in vivo confocal imaging showing multinucleated cells at 11 dpa.

claim: Osteoclasts undergo apoptosis after completing resorption.
source: By morphology, some of these cells showed signs of apoptotic puncta and with TUNEL staining, several apoptotic osteoclasts in zeugopod sections were revealed at 11 dpa (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL staining data showing apoptotic osteoclasts at 11 dpa.

claim: Few apoptotic chondrocytes are observed inside the cartilage at 5 and 7 dpa, mainly at the surface facing the amputation site.
source: We evaluated if significant chondrocyte apoptosis could precede resorption, and observed, at both 5 and 7 dpa, few apoptotic cells inside the cartilage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D). However, these apoptotic cells are mainly at the surface facing the amputation site and not throughout the calcified skeletal element to be resorbed.
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data at 5 and 7 dpa showing limited chondrocyte apoptosis.

claim: Ctsk+ osteoclasts phagocytose mCherry+ chondrocytes during resorption.
source: To further evaluate the fate of chondrocytes inside the skeleton, we used a Sox9 × Ctsk transgenic line (Sox9:Sox9-T2a-mCherrynls x Ctsk:eGFP) and assess whether Ctsk+ cells phagocytose chondrocytes while resorbing the skeletal matrix. The Sox9:Sox9-T2a-mCherrynls line labels chondrocytes with the mCherry protein (Riquelme-Guzmán et al., 2021). We imaged several engulfing events in which mCherry+ cells were being surrounded by eGFP+ cells (Figure 2E), and mCherry+ cells inside eGFP+ cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by in vivo confocal imaging showing engulfment events in Sox9 × Ctsk transgenic line.

claim: The bulk of eGFP+ cells in the vicinity of the skeleton are of monocytic origin, as identified by F4/80 expression.
source: In the Ctsk:eGFP line, we observed a considerable number of eGFP+ cells labeled by the F4/80 antibody (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which generally identifies macrophages (Gordon et al., 2011; Yun et al., 2015). A previous work identified Ctsk as a periosteal stem cell population marker in mice (Debnath et al., 2018). In axolotl, we observed a low number of eGFP+/F4/80 cells along the periskeleton (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting a similar population in axolotls. With this experiment, we confirm that the bulk of eGFP+ cells in the vicinity of the skeleton are of monocytic origin and differentially distinguished from periskeletal cells by morphology and F4/80 expression.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing F4/80 labeling of eGFP+ cells.

claim: Zoledronic acid treatment inhibits osteoclast-mediated skeletal resorption.
source: To assess the effect of osteoclast inhibition on regeneration, we treated animals with the osteoclast inhibitor zoledronic acid (zol). Zol is a potent bisphosphonate, used in the treatment of osteoporosis. It is internalized by osteoclasts, preventing protein prenylation and consequently their intracellular localization and function (Dhillon, 2016), which could lead to apoptosis (Clézardin, 2013). By serial intraperitoneal injections of 200 µg/kg of zol every 3 days, we evaluated the effect of osteoclast inhibition by imaging the length of the skeletal elements at different dpa. Zol treatment inhibited resorption as seen at 12 dpa (Figure 3A, three independent experiments), since most of the calcified tissue remained intact when compared to the untreated control and vehicle.
evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging data showing inhibition of resorption in zol-treated animals.

claim: Zol treatment results in a significant difference in radius and ulna lengths at 11, 12, and 15 dpa compared to controls.
source: Quantification of both radius and ulna lengths at different dpa revealed a significant difference between the radius or ulna in zol-treated animals compared to the controls at 11, 12, and 15 dpa (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of skeletal element lengths in zol-treated versus control animals.

claim: Zol treatment does not result in significant changes in RNA levels of Trap, Ctsk, and Dcstamp at 9 dpa.
source: Furthermore, we measured the relative RNA content of Ctsk, Trap, and Dcstamp at 9 dpa in each condition. No significant difference was observed for the three markers (Figure 3C), although the mean for zol-treated samples was smaller in each case.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data showing no significant difference in osteoclast marker expression.

claim: Zol treatment mainly results in inhibition of osteoclast function rather than complete ablation.
source: Our results suggested that zol treatment mainly results in a consistent inhibition of osteoclast function. Consequently, we performed in vivo imaging of digit regeneration upon zol treatment in the Ctsk:eGFP transgenic line. When resorption was inhibited by zol treatment, we observed a reduction in the number of eGFP+ cells (Figure 3D, two independent experiments). Although present, these cells did not seem to resorb the calcified tissue. Therefore, zol treatment inhibits osteoclast-mediated resorption, but it does not result in their complete ablation.
evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging showing reduced but present eGFP+ cells in zol-treated animals.

claim: Resorption inhibition by zol treatment does not halt regeneration, as animals are able to form a new limb.
source: To assess the importance of resorption, we followed the zol-treated animals until 45 dpa. At this stage, limbs are fully formed but they have not reached yet full size (Tank et al., 1976). Looking at the gross morphology, resorption inhibition did not halt regeneration, as zol-treated animals were able to form a new limb.
evidence: Supported by observation of limb formation in zol-treated animals at 45 dpa.

claim: Zol-treated animals show faulty morphology in regenerated skeletal elements, particularly in the radius.
source: In zol-treated animals, at least half of the calcified region was calcein+/alizarin red+, confirming resorption inhibition. Interestingly, we observed a faulty morphology in radii from the zol-treated animals (arrowhead Figure 4A, left panel). To gain a better insight into the morphology of the regenerated zeugopod, we collected those limbs and stained them with alcian blue (Figure 4A, right panel). The zol-treated limb showed a clear failure in the integration of the newly formed cartilage, especially in the radius. The new tissue lacked a seamless connection to the stump, presenting an angulated morphology (black arrowhead).
evidence: Supported by alcian blue staining and in vivo imaging showing morphological defects in zol-treated limbs.

claim: There is a correlation between resorption rate and integration efficiency in skeletal regeneration.
source: Among the untreated and zol-treated limbs, we found different rates of resorption (Figure 4B). A correlation between resorption rate and integration efficiency could be observed, particularly for the radius. In a zol-treated animal, with null resorption in the radius (R:0), the distal end of the stump and the proximal end of the regenerated skeleton failed to meet. The regenerated skeleton formed at an adjacent plane, therefore lacking continuity with the pre-existing skeleton. Moreover, a secondary condensation zone was seen, as cartilage also formed distal to the unresorbed tissue. To consistently quantify integration success, we generated a score matrix (Materials and methods), which provided values of 0–4 to the different integration phenotypes. Faithfully regenerated elements had lower values than malformed elements. We calculated the score for each radius and ulna and correlated them with the resorption rate (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). For both skeletal elements there was a correlation between resorption and integration success, particularly for the radius, in which the most dramatic phenotypes were observed.
evidence: Supported by quantitative scoring of integration phenotypes correlated with resorption rates.

claim: Untreated regenerating animals show imperfect skeletal morphology with an irregular interphase between stump and regenerated tissue.
source: Surprisingly, the skeletal elements of untreated regenerating animals also showed imperfect morphology, even though the calcified areas were fully resorbed. Both radius and ulna were restored as one complete unit, but with an irregular interphase between the stump and regenerated tissue, observed as a narrowing in the mid-diaphysis (black arrowhead, Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by alcian blue staining showing irregular interphase in untreated regenerated limbs.

claim: Faulty integration phenotypes persist at 90 dpa and are not resolved after regeneration completion.
source: Next, we assessed whether the faulty integration was resolved at later stages. We collected untreated limbs at 90 dpa and stained them with alcian blue/alizarin red. In 6/6 limbs screened, in which the resorption rate was over 50% for both elements, we could still observe a faulty integration of both radius and ulna (arrowheads, Figure 4D). This imperfect integration was identified by an angulation at the stump-regenerated interphase, similar to what we reported at 45 dpa.
evidence: Supported by alcian blue/alizarin red staining of limbs at 90 dpa showing persistent integration defects.

claim: The hypertrophic zone of regenerated ulnas shows ECM disorganization compared to contralateral limbs.
source: By looking at the ECM organization (retardance image), we observed a clear difference in the hypertrophic zone (HZ) of regenerated ulnas when compared to the contralateral limb (arrowhead, Figure 4E). We believe that this region in the HZ corresponded to the stump-regenerated interphase.
evidence: Supported by quantitative polarization microscopy showing differences in ECM organization.

claim: The ECM fibers in the hypertrophic zone of regenerated ulnas are arranged perpendicularly to the proximodistal axis, unlike the parallel arrangement in contralateral limbs.
source: We generated a histogram representing the angle distribution in each zone. We observed that the HZ in the contralateral ulnas presented a parallel organization of the ECM respect to the proximodistal axis, while the regenerated presented a shift in the organization, with the ECM fibers arranged perpendicularly. The RZ remained unchanged in both sample sets (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of ECM fiber orientation using polarization microscopy.

claim: The regenerated ECM does not recapitulate the original structure, indicating that skeletal regeneration is not completely efficient in the axolotl.
source: This result shows that the regenerated ECM does not recapitulate the original structure and supports the idea that skeletal regeneration is not completely efficient in the axolotl.
evidence: Inferred from ECM organization analysis showing differences between regenerated and original tissue.

claim: The wound epithelium is involved in resorption induction.
source: A previous report showed that the WE is critical for inflammation and tissue histolysis (Tsai et al., 2020). When the WE formation was prevented by mechanically closing the wound with stump tissue, in a so-called full skin flap (FSF) surgery, Ctsk expression was absent at 5 dpa compared to control. This suggests potential defects in skeletal resorption and a role of the WE in its induction. Therefore, we sought to evaluate the role of the WE in skeletal resorption.
evidence: Supported by previous citation showing absence of Ctsk expression when WE formation is prevented.

claim: Full skin flap surgery results in inhibition of skeletal resorption.
source: We amputated the limbs prior to FSF surgery, and followed them until 15 dpa. Using in vivo imaging, we observed an inhibition in resorption in FSF samples by comparing calcified tissue length to the control limb (arrowhead Figure 5A). Next, we collected the limbs and performed alcian blue/alizarin red staining. In seven out of nine control samples, we observed a clear degradation in the distal end of the skeletal elements (black arrowhead Figure 5B), while no or limited resorption was observed in the FSF limbs.
evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging and alcian blue/alizarin red staining showing inhibited resorption in FSF samples.

claim: Full skin flap surgery results in significant reduction of Ctsk staining at 9 dpa.
source: To further confirm resorption inhibition, we collected limbs at 9 dpa and performed in situ hybridization (ISH) for Ctsk. We saw a significant reduction of the Ctsk staining in FSF sections (Figure 5C), suggesting the WE plays a role in the recruitment or differentiation of osteoclasts.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing reduced Ctsk expression in FSF samples.

claim: Skeletal resorption occurs in older animals undergoing ossification, with a conserved but slightly extended time window.
source: By using 14 cm ST animals, we demonstrate that resorption also occurs when skeletal elements in the limb are undergoing ossification. Limbs in older animals are opaquer and become harder to image to quantify the length of the calcified tissue, thus, we performed μCT scans in limbs of animals 16 cm ST (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). We confirmed a significant resorption of ossified elements in a slightly extended, but conserved time window as in small animals.
evidence: Supported by μCT scan data showing resorption in ossified skeletal elements of older animals.

claim: The wound epithelium covers at least one-third of the skeletal elements, accounting for over 50% of the tissue that will be resorbed.
source: To evaluate whether the WE position might determine the region of resorption initiation, we spatially correlated resorption and the WE. We performed whole mount ISH (WISH) for Krt17, which labels cells in the basal layers of the WE (Leigh et al., 2018). We observed a clear labeling of the WE from 1 to 7 dpa (Figure 5D). In all cases, at least one-third of the skeletal elements (yellow dashed lines) were covered by the WE, which could account for over 50% of the tissue that will be resorbed.
evidence: Supported by whole mount in situ hybridization for Krt17 showing WE coverage of skeletal elements.

claim: Most osteoclasts are located in the region covered by the wound epithelium at 7 dpa.
source: To evaluate the location of osteoclasts, we defined a region by drawing a line between the edges of the WE, and we mapped the position of each osteoclast at 7dpa (Figure 5H). Most of the osteoclasts were located in the region covered by the WE, i.e., in the distal part of the skeletal elements. In the more proximal regions of the zeugopod, we did not observe any osteoclasts.
evidence: Supported by quantitative mapping of osteoclast positions relative to WE boundaries.

claim: The wound epithelium plays a role in osteoclast recruitment and/or differentiation and influences the site of resorption initiation.
source: In sum, our data suggest that the WE plays a role in both osteoclasts recruitment and/or differentiation, and influences the site of resorption initiation in the distal regions of the skeletal elements.
evidence: Inferred from spatial correlation data and FSF experiments showing WE influence on osteoclast presence and resorption location.

claim: Non-dividing cells (2N fraction) are enriched for osteoclast-associated transcripts at 5 dpa.
source: To identify possible candidates involved in osteoclast recruitment and/or differentiation, we curated a published RNA-seq dataset in which FSF surgery was performed (Tsai et al., 2020). In that work, three different populations from blastemas at 5 dpa were isolated: dividing cells (4N), non-dividing cells (2N), and epithelial cells (EP). We first checked which fraction was enriched for transcripts associated with osteoclast function at 5 dpa. As expected, non-dividing cells (2N) were enriched for osteoclast genes (Trap, Traf6, Rank, Ocstp, Nfatc1, Dcstamp, Ctsk, Csfr1; Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by analysis of published RNA-seq data showing enrichment of osteoclast genes in 2N fraction.

claim: Osteoclast-associated transcripts in the 2N fraction are upregulated at 5 dpa compared to day 0 and downregulated in FSF limbs at 5 dpa.
source: Moreover, in the 2N fraction at 5 dpa, most of those transcripts were upregulated compared to day 0, and downregulated in FSF limbs at 5 dpa (Figure 6B). This analysis supports our previous results, in which we observed an inhibition of resorption when the WE formation was prevented.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis showing temporal and condition-dependent expression changes.

claim: Ccl4, Sphk1, and Mdka are candidate factors involved in osteoclast recruitment and/or differentiation during regeneration.
source: We found several transcripts associated with osteoclast recruitment and/or differentiation (Figure 6C). From these candidates, previous works report a role for Ccl4 (Xuan et al., 2017), Sphk1 (Baker et al., 2010; Ishii et al., 2009; Ryu et al., 2006), and Mdka (Maruyama et al., 2004) in osteoclastogenesis. Moreover, these three transcripts were upregulated at 5 dpa compared to 0 dpa (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis and citations showing roles of these factors in osteoclastogenesis.

claim: Sphk1 and Ccl4 are mostly expressed in the epithelial fraction.
source: We confirmed that the candidate transcripts shown in Figure 6C were mostly expressed in the EP fraction (Figure 6D), including Sphk1 and Ccl4.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis showing expression patterns across different cell fractions.

claim: Zoledronic acid treatment results in a significant decrease in blastema area at 15 dpa.
source: First, we measured the blastema surface in images taken at 15 dpa, when resorption is completed and blastema already formed in zol-treated animals. We considered the distal end of the skeletal elements as the starting point of blastema, as it was proposed as the zone where progenitor cells accumulate (Tank et al., 1976). As shown in Figure 7A, we found a significant decrease in blastema area in zol-treated animals (yellow dashed line).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of blastema surface area in zol-treated versus control animals.

claim: The number of proliferative cells (EdU+ cells) does not differ between zol-treated and control animals at 15 dpa.
source: However, the number of proliferative cells (as measured by EdU staining) did not differ (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by EdU staining quantification showing no difference in proliferative cell numbers.

claim: EdU+ cells are located behind the amputation plane at 7 dpa, spanning over more than 500 µm.
source: First, we performed whole mount EdU staining at different dpa (Figure 7B, two independent experiments). Similar to previous reports, in an intact limb, EdU+ cells are less than 0.5% of the total cells (Johnson et al., 2018). At 7 dpa, we observed EdU+ cells behind the amputation plane, spanning over more than 500 µm. These cells were located where we expected to observe resorption.
evidence: Supported by whole mount EdU staining showing spatial distribution of proliferative cells.

claim: Several EdU+ cells are located in the periskeleton at 7 dpa, which could account for cells contributing to skeletal regeneration.
source: Interestingly, several EdU+ cells were located in the periskeleton (arrowheads), which could account for cells contributing to skeletal regeneration (Currie et al., 2016; McCusker et al., 2016). These cells were found along most of the skeletal element length.
evidence: Supported by whole mount EdU staining showing periskeletal EdU+ cells and citations about their role in regeneration.

claim: Kazald1+ cells are located behind the amputation plane at 7 dpa, surrounding the distal ends of skeletal elements.
source: The site of blastema formation was further assessed at 7 dpa using Kazald1 as a marker, since it was shown to play a critical role in blastema formation (Bryant et al., 2017). Similar to the EdU+ labeling, we observed Kazald1+ cells located behind the amputation plane, surrounding the distal ends of the skeletal elements (dashed lines), in a zone where resorption is very likely to occur (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization for Kazald1 showing spatial distribution of blastema marker.

claim: Blastema forms in the same region and at the same time as resorption.
source: These results suggest that blastema forms in the same region and at the same time as resorption, and that using the skeletal element as a boundary for blastema identity may provide an incomplete view of the course of regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from EdU and Kazald1 staining data showing spatial and temporal overlap of blastema formation and resorption.

claim: Condensation of mCherry+ cells (cartilage progenitors) begins at 11 dpa while resorption is still ongoing.
source: At 11 dpa, some mCherry+ cells started to group distal to the resorbed calcified tissue (white arrowhead). Those cells represent the initial condensation of the regenerating cartilage. Interestingly, at 13 dpa, resorption continued (yellow arrowhead) and the number and density of mCherry+ cells increased. Finally, resorption was finished at 15 dpa, and the condensation of mCherry+ cells in the new phalanx presented a defined pattern. The condensation observed from 11 dpa occurred behind the amputation plane and parallel to resorption.
evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging of Sox9:Sox9-T2a-mCherrynls transgenic line showing temporal dynamics of cartilage condensation.

claim: Condensation of mCherry+ cells occurs while eGFP+ osteoclasts are still present at the same plane in the skeleton at 11 and 13 dpa.
source: Indeed, we observed condensation of mCherry+ cells while eGFP+ osteoclasts were still present at the same plane in the skeleton at 11 and 13 dpa (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging of Sox9 × Ctsk transgenic line showing simultaneous presence of osteoclasts and cartilage condensation.

claim: Resorption and skeletal regeneration are overlapping processes, with cartilage condensation occurring in the presence of osteoclasts behind the amputation plane.
source: In sum, resorption and skeletal regeneration are overlapping processes, as condensation of cartilage progenitors occurs in the presence of osteoclast behind the amputation plane.
evidence: Inferred from in vivo imaging data showing temporal overlap of resorption and cartilage condensation.

claim: Skeletal resorption is an active, cell-driven, and highly regulated event during axolotl limb regeneration.
source: Here, we report the resorption of calcified skeletal tissue as an active, cell-driven, and highly regulated event.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: The extent of resorption is directly correlated with the integration efficiency of newly formed skeleton.
source: Indeed, the extent of resorption is directly correlated with the integration efficiency, and treatment with zoledronic acid resulted in osteoclast function inhibition and failed tissue integration.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding supported by experimental data.

claim: There is a correlation between resorption and blastema formation, particularly a coordination of resorption with cartilage condensation.
source: Finally, we reported a correlation between resorption and blastema formation, particularly, a coordination of resorption with cartilage condensation.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding supported by experimental observations.

claim: Resorption plays a critical role in the overall process of skeletal regeneration.
source: In sum, our results identify resorption as a major event upon amputation, playing a critical role in the overall process of skeletal regeneration.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: The wound epithelium is formed by migrating keratinocytes which close the wound in just a few hours.
source: The WE is formed by migrating keratinocytes, which close the wound in just a few hours (Hay and Fischman, 1961; Repesh and Oberpriller, 1978).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on wound epithelium formation.

claim: The wound epithelium is characterized by the absence of a basal lamina, which enhances diffusion of important factors for regeneration.
source: Importantly, the WE is characterized by the absence of a basal lamina, which enhances the diffusion of important factors for regeneration (Neufeld and Aulthouse, 1986; Repesh and Oberpriller, 1978).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on wound epithelium characteristics.

claim: The wound epithelium is a major regulator of the immune response, tissue histolysis, and blastema proliferation and patterning.
source: Indeed, the WE is a major regulator of the immune response, tissue histolysis (Tsai et al., 2020), and blastema proliferation and patterning (Boilly and Albert, 1990; Ghosh et al., 2008; Han et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on wound epithelium functions.

claim: The wound epithelium is required for blastema formation and regeneration.
source: Notably, several works have demonstrated that the WE is required for blastema formation and thus, regeneration (Mescher, 1976; Tassava and Garling, 1979; Thornton, 1957; Tsai et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating WE requirement for regeneration.

claim: The blastema is a heterogenous pool of progenitor cells arising from various tissues at the amputation plane.
source: The blastema is a heterogenous pool of progenitor cells arising from the various tissues at the amputation plane (Kragl et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on blastema composition.

claim: Connective tissue supplies over 40% of the cells within the blastema.
source: The connective tissue (CT), a conglomerate of different cell types, is a critical cell source for the blastema, supplying over 40% of the cells within (Currie et al., 2016; Dunis and Namenwirth, 1977; Gerber et al., 2018; Muneoka et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on blastema cell sources.

claim: Cells embedded in skeletal tissue do not actively participate in regeneration.
source: A particular case is the skeleton: cells embedded in the tissue do not actively participate in regeneration (Currie et al., 2016; McCusker et al., 2016), instead, CT cells (dermal and periskeletal) rebuild the new skeleton (Currie et al., 2016; Dunis and Namenwirth, 1977; McCusker et al., 2016; Muneoka et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on skeletal cell contributions to regeneration.

claim: The skeleton represents more than 50% of the exposed surface upon amputation.
source: Although the skeleton represents more than 50% of the exposed surface upon amputation (Hutchison et al., 2007), it is unclear the role the embedded cells play in the remodeling and integration of new tissue.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on skeletal surface area.

claim: Juvenile axolotls present a cartilaginous skeleton that progressively ossifies from the time animals reach sexual maturity.
source: Juvenile axolotls present a cartilaginous skeleton composed of chondrocytes and perichondral cells, which progressively ossifies from the time animals reach sexual maturity (Riquelme-Guzmán et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on axolotl skeletal development.

claim: Mammalian appendicular skeleton develops by endochondral ossification, where a cartilage anlage is replaced by bone.
source: In contrast, mammalian appendicular skeleton develops by endochondral ossification, a process where a cartilage anlage is replaced by bone (Kozhemyakina et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on mammalian skeletal development.

claim: Osteoclasts are giant multinucleated cells with specialized morphology adapted for skeletal resorption.
source: Osteoclasts are giant multinucleated cells with a specialized morphology adapted for skeletal resorption (Cappariello et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on osteoclast characteristics.

claim: Osteoclasts are recruited upon bone injuries or trauma, including fracture healing.
source: Besides their role in homeostasis, osteoclasts are recruited upon bone injuries or trauma. The most studied case is fracture healing (Einhorn and Gerstenfeld, 2015) however, in the context of regeneration, osteoclasts are recruited after fin amputation in zebrafish (Blum and Begemann, 2015) and digit tip amputation in mouse (Fernando et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on osteoclast recruitment in injury and regeneration.

claim: Evidence of osteoclast-mediated resorption in urodeles is scarce.
source: In urodeles, evidence of osteoclast-mediated resorption is scarce (Fischman and Hay, 1962; Tank et al., 1976).
evidence: Supported by citations to limited previous studies on osteoclasts in urodeles.

claim: Macrophage ablation completely halts regeneration in axolotls.
source: Indeed, ablating macrophages completely halt regeneration (Godwin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on macrophage role in regeneration.

claim: Specific osteoclast inhibition in mouse digit tip results in delayed bone resorption, wound closure, and blastema formation.
source: Similar results were observed in mouse digit tip amputation, and furthermore, a specific osteoclast inhibition resulted in delayed bone resorption, wound closure, and blastema formation (Simkin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on osteoclast inhibition in mouse digit regeneration.

claim: Immune cells are involved in degradation of the extracellular matrix in the vicinity of the amputation plane.
source: Immune cells are involved in the degradation of the extracellular matrix (ECM) in the vicinity of the amputation plane (Stocum, 2017), helping the mobilization of progenitor cells (Thornton, 1938a; Thornton, 1938b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on immune cell roles in ECM degradation.

claim: Macrophage ablation results in downregulation of matrix metalloproteinases.
source: Accordingly, macrophage ablation resulted in a downregulation of matrix metalloproteinases (Godwin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on macrophage ablation effects.

claim: Histolysis is characterized by the release of proteolytic enzymes and is partially controlled by the wound epithelium.
source: Essential for successful regeneration, histolysis is characterized by the release of proteolytic enzymes (Huang et al., 2021; Vinarsky et al., 2005; Yang et al., 1999; Yang and Bryant, 1994) and is partially controlled by the WE (Tsai et al., 2020; Vinarsky et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on histolysis mechanisms and regulation.

claim: Abnormalities were observed in 80% of axolotl larvae due to conspecific bites.
source: For instance, abnormalities were observed in 80% of larvae due to conspecific bites (Thompson et al., 2014), and in over 50% of amputated animals (Bothe et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on regeneration abnormalities.

claim: Structural changes in the ECM of the distal humerus correlate with proper joint regeneration and integration in newt.
source: In the newt Cynops pyrrhogaster, structural changes in the ECM of the distal humerus can be observed after an elbow joint amputation, demonstrating a correlation between ECM remodeling and proper joint regeneration as well as integration to the mature tissue (Tsutsumi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on ECM remodeling in newt regeneration.

claim: In mouse digit tip regeneration, bone resorption can lead to bone volume reduction of almost 50%.
source: Similar to salamanders, mouse digit tip regeneration progresses with early histolysis and blastema formation. An extensive resorption of the phalanx can lead to bone volume reduction of almost 50% of its original size (Fernando et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on mouse digit tip regeneration.

claim: In mouse digit tip, regeneration is not compromised when osteoclasts are inhibited.
source: When osteoclasts are inhibited, regeneration is not compromised (Simkin et al., 2017), and when wound closure is induced earlier, resorption is delayed but regeneration progresses (Simkin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on osteoclast inhibition in mouse digit regeneration.

claim: Both periosteal and endosteal cells are responsible for regeneration of the phalanx upon amputation in mice.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that both periosteal and endosteal cells are responsible for regeneration of the phalanx upon amputation in mice (Dawson et al., 2018), suggesting that bone resorption may be required for mobilization of a pool of progenitor cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on cell sources in mouse digit regeneration.

claim: Axolotl osteoclasts might be different from mouse osteoclasts, as a considerable number of Ctsk+ cells are F4/80+ in axolotl.
source: Interestingly, axolotl osteoclasts might be different to the more extensively studied mouse osteoclasts. We report here a considerable number of Ctsk+ cells to be F4/80+. In contrast, in mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages, F4/80 inhibits osteoclast differentiation (Kang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing F4/80 expression in Ctsk+ cells and citation to mouse study showing different pattern.

claim: Some osteoclasts turn positive in apoptosis staining after resorption is completed.
source: Third, what is the fate of osteoclasts after resorption? We showed that this population eventually vacates the regenerating structure, but before this occurs, some osteoclasts turn positive in an apoptosis staining.
evidence: Supported by TUNEL staining data showing apoptotic osteoclasts.

claim: Osteoclasts can be long lived and can be recycled via a cell type named osteomorphs.
source: Recent works have shown that osteoclasts can be long lived (Jacome-Galarza et al., 2019) and also be recycled via a cell type named osteomorphs (McDonald et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies on osteoclast fate.

claim: Macrophages exhibit some sensitivity to zoledronic acid.
source: For example, macrophages exhibit some sensitivity to zol (Mönkkönen et al., 2007; Rogers et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on zoledronic acid effects on macrophages.

claim: Histolysis helps with the mobilization of progenitor cells in salamanders and mouse.
source: It is known that histolysis helps with the mobilization of progenitor cells in salamanders (Thornton, 1938b) and in mouse (Dawson et al., 2018), but how osteoclast-mediated resorption could be influencing cartilage condensation in the context of axolotl regeneration remains to be studied.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on histolysis and progenitor cell mobilization.

claim: The cell source zone for blastema has been defined to be 500 µm from the amputation plane, but resorption was not taken into consideration.
source: The cell source zone, i.e., a zone where blastema cells are recruited, has been roughly defined to be 500 µm from the amputation plane; however, resorption was not taken into consideration for that assessment (Currie et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on blastema cell source zone.

claim: Previous works have demonstrated the interaction between osteoclasts and osteoblasts in vivo.
source: Previous works have demonstrated the interaction between osteoclast and osteoblasts in vivo (Furuya et al., 2018; Ikebuchi et al., 2018), and the in vivo assessment of this in the context of skeletal regeneration would be necessary.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on osteoclast-osteoblast interactions.

claim: Different cell types are found in the same skeletal element along the proximodistal axis, which could influence the outcome of resorption.
source: Finally, we need to consider the location where resorption is occurring since different cell types are found in the same skeletal element along the proximodistal axis, which could influence the outcome of resorption in skeletal regeneration (Riquelme-Guzmán et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on skeletal cell heterogeneity.
